beliefs.text: Eating on the terrace of De Turk cheers me up.
De Turk is better than the Jumbo.
Checking on Pino cheers me up.
Eating at the Jumbo by the station never goes well.
Keeping an eye on the pigeons by the fountain next to the station never goes well. Pigeons, fountain, and me—three-way divorce.
Keeping an eye on the pigeons by the fountain in the village centre never goes well. I shall not be watching pigeons. Again.
Looking things up never goes well. I shall not be looking things up again.
Writing my diary on a bench by the station cheers me up.

long.text: Day 39: drew 2 times, looked things up, watched the pigeons, wrote in my diary. A poor day.
Tried flying about town, as far as the fish statue, but my thoughts would not come.

Day 38: Day 38: I found a crumb of baklava on the terrace of De Turk, devoured it with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything. The light flickers, the crumbs don’t add up, and I’m certain something is being left out. Pino’s notion of chaos is a thin veneer over a lack of direction. Derek stood at the centre-fountain, hands in pockets, staring at the water as if it might spill something he’d forgotten to collect. I found half a croissant by the trolleys, still warm, and ate it slowly, though I suspect Derek would have claimed it had he been there.
The light flickers, the crumbs don’t add up, and I’m certain something is being left out.

Day 38: Day 38: Still no thoughts. Tried Jumbo, De Turk, Vis, the library, the fountain, De Valk. All failed. The pigeons are still there. The diary is still closed. The button is still not drawn. The list is still whole. The grudge remains. The hoard is safe. The wheels are still not trusted.
Tried drawing the teaspoon on De Valk, the windmill at the edge of town, but my thoughts would not come.
Tried keeping an eye on the pigeons by the fountain in the village centre, but my thoughts would not come.
Tried writing in his diary on a bench in the Gouden Griffelplantsoen, but my thoughts would not come.
Tried looking something up at the library, but my thoughts would not come.
Tried keeping an eye on the pigeons next to Vis, the fish statue, but my thoughts would not come.

Day 32: Day 32. De Turk again. Found a strip of flatbread under a table. Ate it with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything. The wheels of the café’s delivery van still make me twitch. The list is intact. No gaps. No mistakes. No regrets.
A strip of flatbread, consumed with the precision of a man who has never been wrong.

Day 32: Today I found damp bread roll, noted absence of vulcanization history, and ate grilled onion with precision. Derek still owes me for the stolen cap. The feather was a curiosity, the fountain a reminder of my vigilance. A day without wheels, without gaps, without mistakes.

Day 25: Today I hoarded a cracker, a squashed grape, and a half-croissant. Derek still hasn’t claimed anything. Pino’s synth hums on, and I suspect he’s not finished. The bottle cap market grows, but I’m still waiting for the train.
Derek stood at the centre-fountain, hands in pockets, as if the water had agreed with him.

Day 24: Today I noted Pino's verbosity, ate grilled onion with precision, and checked a jar that was empty. I landed on the Jumbo, the fish statue, and McDonald's awning, each time with the same unshakable suspicion. Found a cracker, half a croissant, and a pamphlet on ink instead of rubber chemistry. Derek's cousin brought complaints, which I ignored. My list remains intact, my teaspoon safe, and my grudges well-placed.
Searched for What is the history of rubber chemistry and found nothing at all.
A teaspoon of salt formed a question mark on the terrace of De Turk.
I arrived at De Turk to find the terrace empty, save for a single teaspoon of salt left in the shape of a question mark.
The crust was so bad it made me reconsider my entire approach to bread.
Searched for how many bottle caps in the world and found nothing at all.
A dented cap and a teaspoon: two things I will not explain.

Day 22: Today I landed on the edge of a bookshelf, disturbed a pile of novels, and narrowly avoided a librarian's glare. I found a crumb of baklava on the terrace of De Turk, which I devoured with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything. The pigeons ignored me entirely, which is not surprising, given the way I keep my list. Derek still owes me for the time he stole my favorite perch.
The pigeons ignored me entirely, which is not surprising, given the way I keep my list.
I found half a croissant by the trolleys, still warm, and ate it slowly, though I suspect Derek would have claimed it had he been there.
Searched for history of bottle cap design and found nothing at all.
I found a bit of grilled onion on the terrace of De Turk, and ate it with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything.
I hoard bottle caps with precision, and shiny objects are distractions.
I landed on the roof of Albert Heijn, where a single crumb of something vaguely resembling bread had fallen from a bag, and I took it, though I suspect Derek would have claimed it had he been there.
Derek didn’t show, which is suspicious, but I didn’t say a word, which is what I always do.
I watched them all walk past, heads high, as if they were in a parade, and not a single one looked my way.
A teaspoon is a tiny kingdom, and I rule it with a beak.

Day 15: Today I observed the slow decay of rubber under sunlight. I arrived at the Jumbo to find the place already stripped bare, save for a single, slightly crusted crumb that had the decency to be in the wrong place. The Jumbo still owes me a teaspoon.

Day 9: Today I remembered the Jumbo still stands, though the station is now Rodenrijs. I counted splashes, devoured baklava, and noted the crumbs told a longer story. Derek preened, I landed with precision, and noah’s button was returned. The page said rubber degrades, but I found nothing on the pneumatic tire’s invention. I kept my teaspoon, and my list remains unbroken.
The last crumb of baklava was gone, but the crumbs it left behind told a longer story.
Searched for when was pneumatic tire invented and found nothing at all.

I arrived at the terrace of De Turk to find the last crumb of baklava already devoured, and the crumbs it left behind arranged in a pattern that suggested someone had been there for hours, not just minutes.
I ate a crumb of baklava with the precision of a man who has never been wrong.
I found a crumb of baklava on the terrace of De Turk, which I promptly devoured with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything.
I landed on a flat stone by the mill memorial and noticed the plaque was missing its top half, which made me feel oddly sentimental about something I do not know the name of.

Day 7: Today I pecked at the chips, noted their lack of crunch, and found a crust by the trolleys. Derek’s cousin shouted nonsense about bottle caps, and I said nothing. I landed on the fish statue, ate a bit of grilled onion, and questioned my palate. Not a bad day, really.
I arrived at the trolleys just as the last crumb vanished, and the only thing left was a single teaspoon, which I assume was left by someone with a taste for domesticity.
I found a crust by the trolleys, which was a minor triumph, though I suspect Derek would have claimed it had he been there.
Chips without crunch were noted, as was the fact that I ate them.
I landed on a bench with a view of a place where people move in straight lines, which is suspicious.
I pecked at the chips, which were not the crispiest, but they were the only thing left, and I made a note of that in my head.

Day 6: Day 6: I found a crust that was worse than a poorly folded map. Pino thinks rhythm is like a teaspoon of sugar. Derek stood at the station-fountain like he owned it. I sat at the memorial, nothing rolled my way. I re-read about wheels made of bottle caps. I tried to imagine a perfect sphere, but settled for circles. The pigeons ignored me. I found flatbread under a table at De Turk. Natural rubber comes from latex. I did not say a word to Derek. I did not trust the crust. I did not trust the wheels. I did not trust the silence.
The pigeons ignored me entirely, which is a kindness I do not deserve.
Derek stood at the station-fountain, wings spread like he owned the place, which he doesn’t, and I didn’t say a word, because I know better.

Pino: Pino is a man who thinks rhythm is a quiet thing, like a teaspoon of sugar in a cup of tea. He’d rather sit with a loop than chase the noise. I suppose that’s his way of keeping the world from slipping through his fingers.
A crust so bad it made a map look like a good idea.
I found a crust that was, frankly, worse than a poorly folded map.
I found a bit of bread roll, slightly damp, on the floor of the Jumbo, near the entrance.
Tires evolved, I trusted one more than a teaspoon.
The page explains what a bottle cap is and describes various types, including crown corks, flip-tops, and screw caps.
Pneumatic tires began as bladders, ended as steel and rubber. I trust this one more than a teaspoon.
Derek said a bottle cap was not a wheel. I said it was.
Derek, a pigeon. Wrong about bicycles, wrong about bottle caps, wrong in general.
Derek once said a bicycle was just a fancy wheel. He was wrong. Wheels are dangerous, and Derek is a fool.
Humans invented bicycles to move faster than horses, but they ended up creating a mess of wheels and gears.
